section-52: Classic definitions: Ogburn said socialization is 'the process by which the individual learns to conform to the norms of the group'; Horton and Hunt described it as the process by which one internalizes the norms of one's groups so that a distinct self emerges, unique to the individual.
Socialization has two sides: from society's point of view, it transmits culture and maintains order; from the individual's point of view, it develops personality and a sense of self.
Cases of children reared in isolation, such as Anna and Isabelle studied by Kingsley Davis, show that without socialization a human being cannot develop normal speech and social behaviour.
section-53: Examples: learning to speak, eat and dress at home (primary); learning rules and discipline at school or office (secondary); a trainee teacher practising teaching (anticipatory); and a person entering the army, a prison or a rehabilitation centre (re-socialization).
Erving Goffman's 'total institutions' (such as prisons and military camps) are settings of intense re-socialization where the old identity is stripped away and a new one is built.
Some textbooks also mention developmental socialization (building on earlier learning) and reverse socialization (the young teaching the old, for example about technology).
section-54: George Herbert Mead described three stages in the development of the self: the preparatory (imitation) stage, the play stage (taking the role of specific others) and the game stage (understanding the 'generalized other').
Following Freud and Parsons, Indian textbooks often list the oral stage, the anal stage, the oedipal stage and adolescence as stages of childhood socialization.
Socialization continues in adulthood (marriage, work, parenthood) and old age (retirement, widowhood), showing that it is lifelong.
section-55: The family teaches language, manners, religion and gender roles; the school teaches knowledge, discipline and citizenship; peer groups teach cooperation and equality and may introduce new values; religion teaches moral codes; and mass media and social media spread ideas and role models.
Other agents include the workplace, the state and law, sports teams and voluntary associations.
In Mizoram, the church, Sunday school, youth fellowships and the YMA are important agents that promote values such as tlawmngaihna and community service.
section-56: Freud explained internalization through the development of the superego, the part of personality that represents society's moral standards and acts as a conscience.
When norms are internalized, people feel guilt or shame when they break them, even if no one else knows. This is why internalization is the most effective form of social control.
Durkheim argued that moral education should help children internalize the values of society so that they feel attached to the group and respect its rules.
section-57: Culture decides what is taught and how it is taught. For example, some cultures emphasize individual achievement and independence, while others emphasize obedience, cooperation and family loyalty.

Margaret Mead's study 'Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies' (1935) in New Guinea suggested that gender behaviour differs across cultures, showing that much of what we consider 'masculine' or 'feminine' is learned through culture.

In Mizo culture, children traditionally learned values such as hospitality, courage, helpfulness and respect for elders through stories, songs, community work and, in the past, the zawlbuk (bachelors' dormitory).
section-58: Socialization helps in the development of self and personality, the learning of language and skills, role learning, the formation of values, the regulation of behaviour and the transmission of culture.
It also prepares individuals for occupations and citizenship, and helps in adjusting to new situations through re-socialization.
Faulty socialization can lead to deviance, delinquency and personality problems, which shows its importance for both the individual and society.
section-59: E.B. Tylor defined culture as 'that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society'.

Bronislaw Malinowski described culture as 'the handiwork of man and the medium through which he achieves his ends'. Robert Bierstedt defined it as 'the complex whole that consists of all the ways we think and do and everything we have as members of society'.
Culture is what distinguishes human beings from animals, since humans rely on learned behaviour rather than instinct.
section-60: Other characteristics include: culture is social, not individual; it satisfies human needs; it is integrated (its parts are connected); it is cumulative (it grows over time); and it varies from society to society.
Culture is symbolic because it depends on language and other symbols to carry meaning. Leslie White argued that symbolling is the basis of all human culture.
Culture is also normative: it provides standards for judging behaviour as right or wrong.
section-61: The distinction between material and non-material culture was made by W.F. Ogburn. Material culture includes houses, tools, machines, clothes and food; non-material culture includes ideas, beliefs, customs, values and language.
Other related types are subculture (the culture of a group within society, such as youth culture), counter-culture (which opposes dominant values), popular culture and high culture.
Examples from Mizoram: the 'puan', bamboo houses and traditional dance instruments are material culture; tlawmngaihna, the Mizo language and customary practices are non-material culture.
section-62: W.F. Ogburn introduced the concept in 'Social Change' (1922). He argued that material culture changes faster because of inventions, while adaptive culture (customs, laws, beliefs) changes more slowly.

Examples: the spread of mobile phones and social media has been faster than the development of norms and laws on privacy, online safety and cybercrime; medical technology has raised ethical issues that law is still addressing.
Cultural lag can lead to social problems and disorganization during periods of rapid change.
section-64: Charles Horton Cooley's 'looking-glass self' explains that the self develops through three steps: we imagine how we appear to others, we imagine their judgement of us, and we develop feelings such as pride or shame as a result.

George Herbert Mead distinguished between the 'I' (the spontaneous, creative part of the self) and the 'me' (the social self formed by internalized expectations). The self develops through play and games in which the child learns to take the role of others.
Different agents dominate at different stages: the family in childhood, the school and peers in adolescence, and the workplace and media in adulthood.

Socialization can fail or be inadequate because of neglect, family conflict or harmful influences. Strong families, good schools and supportive communities are therefore essential for healthy socialization.
section-65: Socialization is not just learning but also the formation of identity. Through interaction, individuals come to see themselves as members of a family, community, religion and nation.
Sigmund Freud's model of personality (id, ego and superego) shows how society's demands, represented by the superego, control biological drives, represented by the id.
Jean Piaget's stages of cognitive development (sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational and formal operational) show that the way children learn depends on their age and mental development.
Socialization is a two-way process: individuals are shaped by society, but they also interpret, resist and change social norms. This is why each generation brings some change to culture.
section-66: Culture includes both 'ideal culture' (the values and norms people say they follow) and 'real culture' (what people actually do). The gap between them is common in every society.

Ethnocentrism is the tendency to judge other cultures by the standards of one's own, while cultural relativism tries to understand each culture in its own context. Culture shock is the confusion experienced when moving into a very different culture.
Cultural change occurs through discovery, invention and diffusion. Acculturation results from continuous contact between cultures, and assimilation is the fuller merging of cultures.

In conclusion, culture is the blueprint of social life; socialization is the process through which individuals learn it; and cultural lag reminds us that different parts of culture change at different speeds.
section-70: Iravati Karve defined the joint family as 'a group of people who generally live under one roof, who eat food cooked at one hearth, who hold property in common, who participate in common family worship and who are related to each other as some particular type of kindred'.

Two schools of Hindu law govern joint family property: Mitakshara (most of India), in which sons acquire a right in ancestral property by birth, and Dayabhaga (Bengal and Assam), in which property passes after the father's death.

I.P. Desai pointed out that jointness is a matter of degree, and he distinguished between residential (household) jointness and functional jointness, where members live separately but cooperate in property, rituals and obligations.
section-71: Characteristics of the joint family include large size, common residence, common kitchen, common property, common worship, authority of the eldest male (the 'karta'), cooperative economy, mutual obligations and subordination of individual interests to the family.

Advantages include social security for the old, the sick and the widowed, division of labour, economy of expenditure, preservation of property and culture, and socialization of children by many elders.
Disadvantages pointed out by critics include restriction of individual freedom, lower status of women, conflicts between members, and a tendency for some members to depend on others.
section-72: Factors of change include industrialization and new occupations, urbanization and lack of space in cities, migration for education and work, Western education and individualistic values, and the changing status and employment of women.

Legislation has also played a role: the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955; the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and its 2005 amendment, which gave daughters equal coparcenary rights in joint family property; and the Special Marriage Act, 1954.
Mass media, new means of transport and communication, and the spread of a cash economy have also weakened the economic basis of the traditional joint family.
section-73: Studies show that the nuclear household has grown, but the extended family remains important for ceremonies, economic help, child care and care of the elderly. A.M. Shah argued that the 'household' and the 'family' should be distinguished, since many families live in several households.
Changes include decline of the authority of elders, greater equality between spouses, more freedom for young people in education and marriage, and smaller families due to family planning.
New problems include the neglect of the elderly, addressed by the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, and the double burden on working women.
section-74: K.M. Kapadia, in 'Marriage and Family in India', said that the aims of Hindu marriage are dharma (religious duty), praja (progeny) and rati (pleasure), with dharma being the most important. Hindu marriage was traditionally regarded as a sacrament (samskara), not a contract.

The ancient texts describe eight forms of Hindu marriage: Brahma, Daiva, Arsha and Prajapatya (approved forms), and Asura, Gandharva, Rakshasa and Paisacha (disapproved forms). Rituals such as kanyadan, panigrahana and saptapadi (seven steps around the sacred fire) are important.

The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, made Hindu marriage monogamous, fixed a minimum age, allowed divorce on specified grounds and permitted inter-caste marriage. Divorce by mutual consent was added in 1976.
section-75: Muslim marriage (nikah) is regarded as a civil contract. Its essential elements include a proposal (ijab) and acceptance (qubul), the consent of both parties, the presence of witnesses, and mahr (dower), which is a sum given by the husband to the wife as a mark of respect and security.

Types of marriage include sahih (valid), batil (void) and fasid (irregular); Shia law also recognizes muta, a temporary marriage. Islamic law permits a man up to four wives under conditions, though monogamy is common in practice.

Divorce may take forms such as talaq (by the husband), khula (initiated by the wife with return of mahr) and mubarat (by mutual consent). The Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939, gave women grounds for divorce. In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court declared instant triple talaq unconstitutional, and the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019, made it void and a punishable offence.
section-76: Christian marriage is considered both a sacrament (especially in the Catholic Church) and a covenant between husband and wife before God. It is monogamous and is ideally lifelong.

The Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872, governs the solemnization of Christian marriages in much of India, and the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 (amended in 2001), governs divorce. Rituals include engagement, publication of banns, a church ceremony, exchange of vows and rings, and blessing by the minister.

In Mizoram, almost all marriages are church weddings combining Christian rites with Mizo customs such as the bride price ('man'). The Mizo Marriage, Divorce and Inheritance of Property Act, 2014, provides the legal framework for marriage and divorce among the Mizo.
section-77: Changes include a rising age at marriage, decline of child marriage, more inter-caste and inter-religious marriages in cities, online matrimonial services, love-cum-arranged marriages, and greater acceptance of divorce and widow remarriage.

Laws such as the Special Marriage Act, 1954, the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, and the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, have shaped marriage practices. However, problems such as dowry deaths and honour killings still occur.
Marriage is gradually moving from being an alliance between families to being a partnership between individuals, though family approval remains important for most Indians.
section-78: G.S. Ghurye, in 'Caste and Race in India' (1932), listed six features of caste: segmental division of society; hierarchy; restrictions on feeding and social intercourse; civil and religious disabilities and privileges of different sections; lack of unrestricted choice of occupation; and restrictions on marriage (endogamy).
The varna system has four categories (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra), while jati refers to the thousands of local endogamous caste groups. Untouchables were placed outside the varna system.
Caste is based on birth and is closed, unlike class, which is more open and based on economic position.
section-79: The Indological or cultural perspective (G.S. Ghurye, Louis Dumont) studies caste through Hindu texts and ideas. Dumont, in 'Homo Hierarchicus' (1966), argued that the opposition between purity and impurity is the basic principle of the caste system.

The structural-functional perspective (M.N. Srinivas) studied caste in villages through fieldwork and developed concepts such as dominant caste, Sanskritization and vote bank. A dominant caste is numerically strong, economically and politically powerful, and has a high ritual status locally.

The conflict and subaltern perspectives (B.R. Ambedkar, Gail Omvedt, Kancha Ilaiah) see caste as a system of exploitation and graded inequality. Ambedkar's 'Annihilation of Caste' (1936) called for the destruction of the caste system. Andre Beteille, in 'Caste, Class and Power' (1965), studied the relationship between caste, class and political power in a Tamil Nadu village.
section-80: Changes include the decline of restrictions on food and social intercourse, the loosening of the link between caste and occupation, legal abolition of untouchability, reservation, and the rise of caste-based political mobilization.
Srinivas observed that caste has become more important in politics even as its ritual aspects decline. Rajni Kothari, in 'Caste in Indian Politics' (1970), discussed the 'politicization of caste'.

Caste persists in matrimony, in local power structures and sometimes in violence and discrimination. Dalit movements and organizations have challenged caste domination and demanded equality and dignity.
section-81: L.P. Vidyarthi and others have divided Indian tribes into zones: the North-Eastern zone (Mizo, Naga, Khasi, Garo, Bodo and others); the Central zone (Gond, Santhal, Munda, Oraon, Ho, Bhil in parts); the Western zone (Bhil, Meena, Warli); the Southern zone (Toda, Irula, Kurumba, Chenchu); and the Island zone (Andaman and Nicobar groups such as the Onge and Jarawa).

Some scholars also identify a Himalayan zone (Gaddi, Bhotia, Lepcha). The central Indian belt has the largest tribal population in absolute numbers, while the North-Eastern states have the highest proportion of tribal people.
Mizoram, Nagaland, Meghalaya and Arunachal Pradesh have tribal majorities, and Lakshadweep also has a predominantly Scheduled Tribe population.
section-82: Colonial forest laws, such as the Indian Forest Acts of 1865 and 1878, declared large forest areas as government property and restricted tribal rights of shifting cultivation, hunting and collection of forest produce.

The colonial land revenue system introduced private ownership of land and brought moneylenders, traders and landlords into tribal areas, leading to land alienation and indebtedness. This contributed to revolts such as the Santhal Hul (1855-56) and the Munda Ulgulan led by Birsa Munda (1899-1900).

In the North-East, the British followed a policy of limited interference. The Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873, introduced the Inner Line, which still regulates entry into Mizoram through the Inner Line Permit. Under the Government of India Act, 1935, the Lushai Hills was declared an 'Excluded Area'.
section-83: Three approaches have been debated: isolation, associated with Verrier Elwin's early view that tribes should be protected in a kind of 'national park'; assimilation, associated with G.S. Ghurye, who described tribes as 'backward Hindus' who should be absorbed into Hindu society; and integration, the policy adopted after independence.

Jawaharlal Nehru's 'Panchsheel' for tribal development (stated in his foreword to Elwin's 'A Philosophy for NEFA') included: people should develop along the lines of their own genius; tribal rights to land and forests should be respected; tribal people should be trained to run their own administration; tribal areas should not be over-administered; and results should be judged by the quality of human character rather than money spent.

Autonomy is provided through the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, PESA (1996), the Forest Rights Act (2006), and special provisions such as Article 371G for Mizoram, which protects Mizo customary law and land ownership.
section-84: Education has been a major force of change, especially in the North-East, where Christian missions introduced schools. Mizoram's high literacy is closely connected with missionary education.

Other factors include the spread of the market economy, improved roads and communication, government development programmes, reservation in jobs and education, urbanization, migration to cities for education and work, and political movements for identity and autonomy.

These changes have produced both opportunities (education, employment, political participation) and challenges (loss of traditional culture, land alienation in some regions, internal inequality among tribes, and identity conflicts).
section-86: Henry Maine described the Indian joint family as a 'patriarchal' unit and thought it would disappear with modernization. Later sociologists showed that it adapted rather than disappeared.

I.P. Desai's study in Mahuva (Gujarat) found that most families had some jointness, even if they lived separately. K.M. Kapadia and others observed that nuclear households often maintain strong ties with the larger family.

Positive changes include greater freedom, equality for women and children, and more democratic decision-making. Negative effects include insecurity for the elderly and loss of traditional support systems.

In Mizoram, families are traditionally patrilineal and smaller than the classic Hindu joint family. The youngest son traditionally stayed with and cared for the parents, while other sons set up their own households. Today, urbanization and government employment have increased nuclear households, while clan and kin ties remain important.
In conclusion, the Indian family is best described as a 'changing but resilient' institution that combines traditional obligations with modern values.
section-87: A comparison: Hindu marriage was traditionally a sacrament, indissoluble and linked with caste and gotra rules; Muslim marriage is a civil contract with mahr and the possibility of divorce; Christian marriage is a sacrament or covenant, monogamous and solemnized in church.

Personal laws governing marriage include the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (also applying to Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists), Muslim personal law, the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939, the Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872, the Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936, and the Special Marriage Act, 1954, for inter-religious and civil marriages.

Article 44 of the Constitution directs the state to endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code for citizens throughout India. This remains a debated issue. Uttarakhand passed a Uniform Civil Code law in 2024.
Common trends across religions include rising age at marriage, decline of polygamy, greater individual choice, legal protection for women and the influence of education and urbanization.
In tribal societies such as the Mizo, marriage is governed by customary law and church practices, showing that India's diversity in marriage extends beyond the major religions.
section-88: Theories of the origin of caste include the traditional theory (divine origin from the 'Purusha Sukta' of the Rig Veda), the racial theory (H.H. Risley, who linked caste with race), the occupational theory (Nesfield), and the political theory (Brahmin domination). Most sociologists believe caste developed through a combination of factors over a long period.
M.N. Srinivas's concepts are important: Sanskritization explains mobility within the caste system; the 'dominant caste' explains village power; and 'vote bank' explains caste in electoral politics.

Factors of change include Western education, industrialization, urbanization, means of transport, legal reforms (abolition of untouchability, reservation), democratic politics, social reform movements and the Dalit movement.

Despite change, caste continues in new forms: caste associations, caste-based political parties, matrimonial preferences and caste-based violence. Andre Beteille noted that caste, class and power have become more separated in modern India, though they still overlap.

In conclusion, caste in contemporary India shows a paradox: its ritual basis is weakening, but its role in identity and politics continues. The constitutional vision is of a society based on equality and dignity for all.
section-89: The Constitution does not define 'tribe', but Article 366(25) refers to Scheduled Tribes as communities specified under Article 342. Census 2011 counted about 10.4 crore Scheduled Tribe persons.

Tribal problems include land alienation, indebtedness, displacement due to dams, mines and industrial projects, low literacy in some regions, poor health and nutrition, loss of forest rights, and exploitation by outsiders. The Xaxa Committee (2014) studied the socio-economic, health and educational status of tribal communities.

Tribal movements have ranged from agrarian and forest-based struggles to political movements for autonomy and statehood, such as the movements that led to the creation of Mizoram (state in 1987), Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh (2000).

In Mizoram, the Mizo National Front movement and the 1986 Mizo Peace Accord led to statehood. Article 371G protects Mizo religious and social practices, customary law, administration of civil and criminal justice according to Mizo customary law, and ownership and transfer of land.
Tribal development requires respect for culture, participation of the people in planning, protection of land and forest rights, education in mother tongue, health care and sustainable livelihoods.
section-92: MacIver and Page said social change refers to changes in social relationships. Kingsley Davis defined it as 'only such alterations as occur in social organization, that is, the structure and functions of society'. Morris Ginsberg described it as 'a change in social structure'.

Social change is distinct from cultural change, though they overlap. Kingsley Davis noted that cultural change is broader, including changes in art, science, technology and philosophy, while social change is a part of it.
Examples of social change in India include the decline of untouchability, changing status of women, growth of nuclear families and the spread of education.
section-93: Characteristics: social change is universal; it is a community change, not merely individual change; its speed differs across societies and periods; it is difficult to predict; it is often a chain reaction because a change in one part affects others; and it is value-neutral (neither good nor bad in itself).
Change may be planned (such as land reform, family planning and Panchayati Raj) or unplanned (such as the effects of natural disasters or technological diffusion).
The pace of change has increased greatly in modern times due to science, technology, communication and globalization.
section-94: Progress is change in a desired direction, judged according to values. Since values differ, what is progress for one group may not be progress for another. MacIver said progress implies 'not merely direction but direction towards some final goal'.

Development has economic and social dimensions. Economic development refers to growth in income and production, while human development, as measured by the UNDP's Human Development Index (introduced in 1990), includes health, education and standard of living.

Amartya Sen's 'Development as Freedom' (1999) defines development as the expansion of people's real freedoms. Sustainable development, defined in the Brundtland Report (1987), means meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
section-95: Evolution comes from the Latin 'evolvere' meaning 'to unfold'. Social evolution refers to a process of gradual change from simple to complex. Herbert Spencer applied Darwin's idea of evolution to society.

Revolution involves sudden, radical and often violent change in political, economic or social structure. Examples include the French Revolution (1789), the Russian Revolution (1917) and the Chinese Revolution (1949). The Industrial Revolution was a revolution in technology and economy, though it took place over decades.
Some scholars also discuss reform, which is planned, gradual and peaceful change within the existing system, such as social reform movements in India.
section-96: Obstacles include: traditionalism and fear of the new; vested interests of groups who benefit from existing arrangements; ignorance and illiteracy; superstitions; caste, religious and kinship restrictions; economic constraints; geographical isolation; and the 'habit' of following customs.
Psychological factors such as fear of the unknown and resistance to new ideas are also important. Administrative obstacles include poor implementation and corruption.
Change agents such as education, mass media, social movements and leadership help to overcome these obstacles.
section-97: W.F. Ogburn is the main exponent of the technological theory of change; he argued that inventions in material culture are the main cause of social change, producing cultural lag. Karl Marx also emphasized technology when he wrote that 'the hand-mill gives you society with the feudal lord; the steam-mill, society with the industrial capitalist'.

Examples of technological change: the steam engine and factory system led to urbanization; the printing press spread literacy; the automobile and railways increased mobility; and the internet and smartphones have transformed communication, business, education and politics.

In India, initiatives such as Digital India (2015), Aadhaar, UPI payments and online education show how technology is transforming society, but the 'digital divide' between urban and rural, rich and poor also creates new inequalities.
section-98: Education is regarded as the most important agent of planned social change. It changes attitudes, removes superstitions, creates awareness of rights, promotes mobility and prepares people for new occupations.

The Indian Constitution made free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 a fundamental right under Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002), implemented through the Right to Education Act, 2009. The National Education Policy, 2020, aims for universal access, multidisciplinary learning and skill development.
In Mizoram, mission education from the late nineteenth century led to rapid literacy and the emergence of an educated middle class, showing the transformative power of education.
section-99: Max Weber showed in 'The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism' that religious ideas can promote social change, in contrast to Marx's emphasis on economic factors.

Cultural factors of change include new ideas and ideologies (such as democracy, nationalism, socialism and feminism), religious reform movements, cultural contact through migration and media, and changes in values about family, gender and individual rights.

In India, social reform movements such as the Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj, and the work of reformers such as Raja Ram Mohan Roy, Jyotirao Phule and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar challenged practices like sati, child marriage and caste discrimination.
section-100: Karl Marx is the main exponent of economic determinism. He argued that the economic base (the forces and relations of production) shapes the superstructure (law, politics, religion, family, culture). When the forces of production change, they come into conflict with existing relations of production, leading to social change.

Examples of economic change: industrialization creating a working class; the Green Revolution changing agrarian relations; liberalization since 1991 creating new middle classes and consumer culture; and the growth of the service sector and IT industry.
Economic factors interact with others, so many sociologists reject pure economic determinism but accept that economic change is a powerful force.
section-101: Auguste Comte's Law of Three Stages (theological, metaphysical, positive) is an early evolutionary theory. Herbert Spencer described evolution from simple, homogeneous societies to complex, heterogeneous ones and used the phrase 'survival of the fittest'.

Lewis Henry Morgan, in 'Ancient Society' (1877), described three stages of human development: savagery, barbarism and civilization. Durkheim described a change from mechanical solidarity to organic solidarity as the division of labour increased.

Criticisms: early evolutionary theories assumed all societies follow the same path and treated Western society as the highest stage. Neo-evolutionists such as Talcott Parsons and Gerhard Lenski later offered more careful versions.
section-102: Talcott Parsons viewed society as a system in equilibrium. Change occurs when one part of the system changes, creating strain, and the system adjusts to restore balance. He described the processes of evolutionary change as differentiation, adaptive upgrading, inclusion and value generalization.
Robert K. Merton's idea of dysfunctions shows that some elements can create strain and lead to change.
Criticism: functional theory is said to explain stability better than change and to neglect conflict and power.
section-103: Karl Marx argued that 'the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles' (The Communist Manifesto, 1848). He saw change occurring through the conflict between classes, such as feudal lords and serfs or capitalists and workers, leading to new forms of society.

Ralf Dahrendorf, in 'Class and Class Conflict in Industrial Society' (1959), argued that conflict arises from unequal distribution of authority, not only property. Lewis Coser showed that conflict can have positive functions, such as promoting change and strengthening group solidarity.
Conflict theory helps explain social movements, revolutions, trade union struggles, caste movements and women's movements.
section-104: Oswald Spengler, in 'The Decline of the West' (1918-1922), compared civilizations to living organisms that pass through birth, growth, maturity and decay. He predicted the decline of Western civilization.

Arnold J. Toynbee, in 'A Study of History', explained the rise and fall of civilizations through 'challenge and response': civilizations grow when a creative minority responds successfully to challenges, and decline when they fail.

Pitirim Sorokin, in 'Social and Cultural Dynamics' (1937-1941), described societies fluctuating between ideational culture (based on faith and spiritual values), sensate culture (based on the senses and material values) and an intermediate idealistic culture. Vilfredo Pareto's theory of the 'circulation of elites' (between 'lions' and 'foxes') is also cyclical.
section-105: Srinivas introduced the term in 'Religion and Society among the Coorgs of South India' (1952). He first called it 'Brahminization' but later used Sanskritization because the reference model could also be Kshatriya, Vaishya or other locally dominant castes.

Sanskritization involves adopting practices such as vegetarianism, teetotalism, wearing the sacred thread, Sanskritic rituals and restrictions on widow remarriage. Srinivas noted that it leads to 'positional change' within the caste hierarchy, not a structural change in the system itself.

Critics pointed out that it can reinforce caste hierarchy and patriarchal practices. Yogendra Singh discussed it in 'Modernization of Indian Tradition' (1973), and some scholars have noted 'de-Sanskritization' movements that reject upper-caste models, such as the non-Brahmin movement in South India.
section-106: Srinivas, in 'Social Change in Modern India' (1966), defined Westernization as 'the changes brought about in Indian society and culture as a result of over 150 years of British rule, the term subsuming changes occurring at different levels: technology, institutions, ideology and values'.
Westernization influenced dress, food habits, language (English), education, law, the press, railways, the bureaucracy, and values such as humanitarianism, rationalism and equality.

It was first adopted by upper castes and urban elites, then spread more widely. Sanskritization and Westernization could occur together, and Srinivas noted that Westernization also encouraged Sanskritization by spreading means of communication.
section-107: Srinivas described secularization in India as a process in which 'what was previously regarded as religious is now ceasing to be such', with increased rationalism and differentiation of institutions.

Indicators of secularization include: the decline of religious control over education, law and politics; the rise of scientific explanation; the decline of purity-pollution rules in public places; and greater rationality in everyday life.

Secularization is different from secularism. Secularization is a social process; secularism is a political principle about the relationship between state and religion. In India, religion continues to play an important role in public life, so secularization has been partial.
section-108: Modernization involves industrialization, urbanization, the spread of education and mass media, scientific outlook, democratic institutions, social mobility, and rational-legal bureaucracy. Daniel Lerner, in 'The Passing of Traditional Society' (1958), emphasized empathy and mobility as features of modern personality.

Yogendra Singh, in 'Modernization of Indian Tradition' (1973), argued that Indian modernization does not mean the complete replacement of tradition but an adaptive process in which tradition and modernity coexist.

Critics argued that early modernization theory equated modernity with Westernization and ignored the different paths of non-Western societies. Concepts such as 'multiple modernities' highlight these different paths.
section-110: Social change can be studied at different levels: micro (changes in individual attitudes and interaction), meso (changes in organizations and communities) and macro (changes in institutions and whole societies).
Patterns of change include linear (progress in one direction), cyclical (repeated cycles of rise and fall) and fluctuating (oscillation between opposite tendencies).

Planned social change in India has been pursued through the Five Year Plans, land reforms, Panchayati Raj, reservation, rural development programmes and social legislation. NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015.

In Mizoram, social change has been rapid since the late nineteenth century: conversion to Christianity, mission education, the decline of chieftainship (abolished in 1954), political mobilization, statehood (1987), urbanization and globalization have transformed society, though values such as tlawmngaihna continue.
In conclusion, social change is inevitable, but its direction and speed depend on the interaction of many factors and on human choices and policies.
section-111: Other factors include demographic factors (population growth, migration, age structure), biological factors, environmental and geographical factors (climate, natural disasters), political factors (laws, state policies, revolutions) and ideological factors (new ideas and social movements).

Theorists emphasize different factors: Marx emphasized economic factors; Weber emphasized religious and cultural ideas; Ogburn emphasized technology; and environmental determinists emphasized geography.

Most sociologists today adopt a multi-causal or pluralistic approach. For example, the changing status of women in India results from education, economic participation, legal reform, women's movements, media and technology working together.
Students should explain each factor with examples, and conclude that social change results from the interaction of several factors, not from a single cause.
section-112: Evolutionary theory (Comte, Spencer, Morgan, Durkheim): change is gradual and moves from simple to complex. Criticism: it assumes a single path and Western superiority.

Functional theory (Parsons, Merton): society is a system that adjusts to maintain equilibrium; change happens through differentiation and adaptation. Criticism: it neglects conflict and sudden change.
Conflict theory (Marx, Dahrendorf, Coser): change results from struggles between groups over power and resources. Criticism: it may overemphasize conflict and economic factors.
Cyclical theory (Spengler, Toynbee, Sorokin, Pareto): societies pass through recurring cycles of growth and decline. Criticism: it is often speculative and difficult to test.
Each theory explains some aspects of social change. A comprehensive understanding combines insights from all of them.
section-113: Srinivas's concepts help explain change in caste society: Sanskritization explains mobility within the system, while Westernization explains change arising from British contact. Yogendra Singh distinguished between 'orthogenetic' change (from within the tradition) and 'heterogenetic' change (from contact with other cultures).
Secularization has affected education, law and public life, though religion remains important. Modernization involves the growth of science, technology, democracy, education and urbanization.

These processes often overlap. For example, a family may adopt modern education and occupations (Westernization and modernization), become less bound by ritual rules (secularization), and also adopt certain high-caste customs (Sanskritization).
In tribal societies of the North-East, such as the Mizo, change has come more through Christianization, mission education, Westernization and modernization than through Sanskritization.
In conclusion, Indian society shows a mixture of tradition and modernity. Students should define each process, mention its features and examples, discuss criticisms and show how they interact.
